newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Could France push Germany to the brink on EMU?.
newsitem.headline: Could France push Germany to the brink on EMU?.

text.p: How far is Germany prepared to go to see the European single currency launched on time is the key question raised by the prospect of a victory for the left in Sunday's French general elections.

French Socialist leader Lionel Jospin favours a flexible interpretation of the Maastricht criteria for monetary union, raising concerns about the credibility of the euro if the French left ousts the ruling centre-right government.

Analysts say it has become unquestionably clear that Bonn, which has repeatedly called for strict implementation of the Maastricht criteria to ensure the euro's credibility, has had to swallow a great deal in recent months to ensure that EMU goes ahead on schedule in 1999.
But whether it is willing to roll over entirely is open to renewed debate and speculation.
"I don't think the Germans would accept anything...There are circumstances where they could back off," says Bruce Kasman, European economist at J.P. Morgan in London.
"We are getting to the limits," added David Marsh, European strategist at Robert Fleming in London.
"There are basically two outcomes. One is to have very wide membership in the euro and the other is to have the whole project abandoned. Two week ago neither of those outcomes were likely."

The possibility of a postponment had recently receded after a series of events and decisions that seemed to show that the achievement of the euro as an absolute political necessity, especially in Germany.
Many believe that the single currency project is at or near the point of no return, with no going back on the euro.

Th most important was Chancellor Helmut Kohl's decision to stand for re-election in 1998. Before this announcement there were widespread doubts about Bonn's commitment to EMU, with talk of a postponement surfacing nearly every day.

Kohl's decision was followed by German Finance Minister Theo Waigel's desperate raid on the Bundesbank's gold reserves, a strategy designed to plug a large hole in the government's 1997 revenue stream.

It is still unclear whether the plan, intended to revalue the reserves at market prices, will be allowed under European accounting rules. At a minimum, analysts say it has badly tarnished Germany's credibility and weakened its bargaining position over who will join the euro in 1999.

Now comes a potential upheaval in France's government, with a Socialist and Communist coalition possibly gaining parliamentary control. Jospin has made it clear that further austerity measures will not be forthcoming should France fall short of the Maastricht budget deficit criteria.

And while a left-wing victory is the greatest worry among analysts, there is also concern that a wafer-thin majority of the French centre-right, led by the newly converted EMU supporter Phillipe Seguin, would be less committed to a strict application of Maastricht critiera.
Therefore flexibility in the interpreation of Maastricht is likely to become all the rage, particularly given Bonn's own resort to fiscal gimmickry.
"Our German friends, who are so rigorous about the criteria, are looking to see if they can't fudge things," Jospin told French radio on Wednesday.
The immediate upshot of a potential Socialist win is that there would be a greater chance of EMU taking off with a much larger number of countries, possibly even Italy.
"The outcome of the French elections will certainly have an impact on the group of countries that will join EMU in 1999," says Peter Cornelius, economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Frankfurt.
"We see a much larger chance for Italy to join EMU right from the beginning."

Analysts say all of these developments must rattle the nerves of fiscally austere Bundesbank officials and some believe Bonn is taking a huge gamble with public opinion and Germany's Constitutional Court.
The latter must rule on the whether EMU abides by the Maastricht critiera in a rigorous fashion.
"I don't know anymore where the Germans will draw the line," says Thomas Mayer, economist at Goldman Sachs in Frankfurt.
"But they are clearing running risks with the public and the Constitutional Court."

German public opinion towards EMU has been anything but supportive and if France's electoral outcome suggests a large element of fatigue with the single currency, experts say it might be advisable for Bonn to draw a few lessons.
Pressing ahead with a single currency at any cost is a gambit that might backfire politically.
"Kohl has an interest for currency union to start, but on the surface it has to be stable," says Hans-Guenter Redeker of Chase Manhattan Bank.
"If it has the smell of being unstable I don't think he has a chance of surviving in the next election."
